gap: No result ChatGPT got normalises BLUETTI's cycle ratings into a cost per rated lifetime kWh (Elite 200 V2 about $0.072/kWh against about $0.122 for the Elite 100 V2, both counted to 80% retention at today's US store prices), or says that the Elite 200 V2's 3,900 W figure, which reviewers list as 'max surge', is a resistive-only Lifting Power number by BLUETTI's own US page. That leaves 2,600 W continuous as its only stated rating for fridge and pump starts.
standout_why: I compared against OutdoorGearLab's AC180 review (cited). It gives a '2700 watt surge rating' without saying it is Power Lifting, a 20 ms UPS time, and 950 Wh usable, but no cycle life. preparedstates.com (top result, not cited) lists maker cycle counts (Elite 100 V2 4,000, AC180 3,500, Elite 200 V2 6,000) without retention percentages. It marks the Elite 200 V2 'Lifting power only' and says once that lifting power is 'for resistive loads like kettles and heaters', but it never works out a cost per lifetime kWh. It also lists the Elite 100 V2 at '3,600 W surge', which conflicts with BLUETTI's 2,700 W Lifting Power. The Gadgeteer, which wasn't among the results, lists 3,900 W as 'Max Surge Power'. The cited Yahoo/CNET page returned HTTP 403 and I could not read it, so I am going on ChatGPT's summary (81.08% efficiency, 26 h 32 min fridge run), which has none of this. So rivals have part of the lifting-power point, and the lifetime-cost normalisation and the UPS-time spread (≤10 / 15 / 20 ms) are new.
decides: This confirms the Elite 200 V2 as the value pick for anyone who cycles the battery often or keeps it for home backup. On BLUETTI's own '80% original capacity' figures it costs about 41% less per rated lifetime kWh than the Elite 100 V2. The lifting-power footnote is the caveat: for a fridge or well-pump start, size on 2,600 W continuous, not 3,900 W. The AC180 no longer counts as a 'discounted older-model option'. It now sells for the same $499 as the Elite 100 V2 and works out the same per lifetime kWh (about $0.124). Against that, it weighs 37 lb vs 25 lb, has a 20 ms UPS switchover vs ≤10 ms, and BLUETTI's 3,500-cycle rating carries no retention percentage. So the Elite 100 V2 stays the 1 kWh pick, and the AC180 is only worth it if it goes well below $499.
